content.title: HEALTHY COOKING {{MISTAKES}}
facts: **Olive oil** – Using extra virgin olive oil for high-heat frying isn't automatically bad, but heating it past its smoke point breaks down beneficial compounds; save the best oil for finishing dishes instead.
**Boiling vegetables** – Boiling broccoli and other veggies leaches water-soluble vitamins like vitamin C into the water; steaming preserves far more nutrients.
**Rinsing quinoa** – Skipping the rinse doesn't just affect taste; it leaves behind saponins that cause a bitter, soapy flavor, not a health risk.
**Overcooking garlic** – Browning garlic too quickly turns it bitter and destroys the compound allicin, which needs a few minutes of rest after chopping to form properly.
**Low-fat salad dressing** – Using fat-free dressing on salads actually reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins like **vitamin A, D, E, and K** found in the vegetables.
**Peeling produce** – Peeling apples, cucumbers, and potatoes removes a significant portion of the **fiber** and antioxidants concentrated in the skin.
**Marinating time** – Marinating meat for just a few minutes does little; flavors and tenderizing effects need at least 30 minutes to properly penetrate.
**Salting pasta water** – Adding salt after boiling doesn't season the pasta itself; salt needs to be in the water before cooking to be absorbed.
**Microwaving vegetables** – Contrary to popular belief, microwaving with minimal water often preserves more nutrients than boiling, not fewer.
**Cold-pressed juice** – Believing fresh juice retains all fiber is a myth; juicing removes most of the insoluble fiber found in whole fruits and vegetables.
